claim: Vax1 is expressed in Sox2-positive neural progenitor cells (NPCs) at the vHT of E14.5 mouse embryo.
source: At the vHT of days post coitum 14.5 (E14.5) mouse embryo, Vax1 is expressed in Sox2 (SRY box 2)-positive neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and RC2-detectable nestin-positive radial glia (Figure 1A,B; top rows), which is known to provide RGC axon guidance cues (Petros et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B and cited reference (Petros et al., 2008).

claim: Vax1 is expressed in RC2-detectable nestin-positive radial glia at the vHT of E14.5 mouse embryo.
source: At the vHT of days post coitum 14.5 (E14.5) mouse embryo, Vax1 is expressed in Sox2 (SRY box 2)-positive neural progenitor cells (NPCs) and RC2-detectable nestin-positive radial glia (Figure 1A,B; top rows), which is known to provide RGC axon guidance cues (Petros et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B and cited reference (Petros et al., 2008).

claim: OC-forming cells are present in Vax1-deficient mice.
source: Although the morphology of the chiasm is abnormal in Vax1-deficient (Vax1−/−) mice (Bertuzzi et al., 1999), these OC-forming cells and several chiasm-localized cues (NrCAM and Vegfa) are still present (Figure 1A,B, bottom rows; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and cited reference (Bertuzzi et al., 1999).

claim: NrCAM is still present in Vax1-deficient mice.
source: Although the morphology of the chiasm is abnormal in Vax1-deficient (Vax1−/−) mice (Bertuzzi et al., 1999), these OC-forming cells and several chiasm-localized cues (NrCAM and Vegfa) are still present (Figure 1A,B, bottom rows; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and cited reference (Bertuzzi et al., 1999).

claim: Vegfa is still present in Vax1-deficient mice.
source: Although the morphology of the chiasm is abnormal in Vax1-deficient (Vax1−/−) mice (Bertuzzi et al., 1999), these OC-forming cells and several chiasm-localized cues (NrCAM and Vegfa) are still present (Figure 1A,B, bottom rows; Figure 1—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1, and cited reference (Bertuzzi et al., 1999).

claim: vHT explants from Vax1−/− mice are unable to attract RGC axons regardless of the Vax1 gene status of co-cultured retinal explants.
source: However, vHT explants from Vax1−/− mice were unable to attract RGC axons regardless of the Vax1 gene status of co-cultured retinal explants, whereas wild-type (WT; Vax1+/+) vHT explants were able to attract RGC axons projected from Vax1−/− explants as well as WT explants (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Wild-type vHT explants are able to attract RGC axons projected from Vax1−/− explants.
source: However, vHT explants from Vax1−/− mice were unable to attract RGC axons regardless of the Vax1 gene status of co-cultured retinal explants, whereas wild-type (WT; Vax1+/+) vHT explants were able to attract RGC axons projected from Vax1−/− explants as well as WT explants (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Wild-type vHT explants are able to attract RGC axons projected from WT explants.
source: However, vHT explants from Vax1−/− mice were unable to attract RGC axons regardless of the Vax1 gene status of co-cultured retinal explants, whereas wild-type (WT; Vax1+/+) vHT explants were able to attract RGC axons projected from Vax1−/− explants as well as WT explants (Figure 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 1C,D.

claim: Vax1 controls RGC axonal growth in a non-cell autonomous manner.
source: We therefore concluded that Vax1 controls the RGC axonal growth in a non-cell autonomous manner, potentially by regulating the expression of unidentified secreted axon-guidance molecules.
evidence: Inferred from the co-culture explant experiments showing that vHT Vax1 status, not retinal Vax1 status, determines RGC axon attraction.

claim: RGC axons from retinal explants grew preferentially toward co-cultured Vax1-expressing COS7 cell aggregates.
source: RGC axons from retinal explants grew preferentially toward co-cultured Vax1-expressing COS7 cell aggregates, whereas RGC axons projected in random directions upon co-incubation with untransfected or Vax2-overexpressing COS7 cell aggregates (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: RGC axons projected in random directions upon co-incubation with untransfected COS7 cell aggregates.
source: RGC axons from retinal explants grew preferentially toward co-cultured Vax1-expressing COS7 cell aggregates, whereas RGC axons projected in random directions upon co-incubation with untransfected or Vax2-overexpressing COS7 cell aggregates (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: RGC axons projected in random directions upon co-incubation with Vax2-overexpressing COS7 cell aggregates.
source: RGC axons from retinal explants grew preferentially toward co-cultured Vax1-expressing COS7 cell aggregates, whereas RGC axons projected in random directions upon co-incubation with untransfected or Vax2-overexpressing COS7 cell aggregates (Figure 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Vax2 shares an identical homeodomain with Vax1.
source: Because Vax2 shares an identical homeodomain with Vax1 (Barbieri et al., 1999), these results indicate that the RGC axon growth stimulatory activity is specific for Vax1.
evidence: Supported by cited reference (Barbieri et al., 1999).

claim: The RGC axon growth stimulatory activity is specific for Vax1.
source: Because Vax2 shares an identical homeodomain with Vax1 (Barbieri et al., 1999), these results indicate that the RGC axon growth stimulatory activity is specific for Vax1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vax2, despite sharing an identical homeodomain, does not stimulate RGC axon growth like Vax1.

claim: Vax1(R152S)-expressing COS7 cells are able to induce RGC axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-expressing COS7 cells.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that Vax1(R152S)-expressing COS7 cells were also able to induce RGC axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-expressing COS7 cells (Figure 2A, third row, B), suggesting that Vax1 induces RGC axonal growth in a transcription-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by co-culture data shown in Figure 2A,B.

claim: Vax1 induces RGC axonal growth in a transcription-independent manner.
source: Unexpectedly, we found that Vax1(R152S)-expressing COS7 cells were also able to induce RGC axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-expressing COS7 cells (Figure 2A, third row, B), suggesting that Vax1 induces RGC axonal growth in a transcription-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S) mutant induces RGC axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1.

claim: Vax1 and Vax1(R152S) proteins are detectable in NF160-positive RGC axons projecting from co-cultured retinal explants.
source: More strikingly, Vax1 and Vax1(R152S) proteins were not only expressed in transfected COS7 cells, they were also detectable in neurofilament 160 kDa (NF160)-positive RGC axons projecting from co-cultured retinal explants (Figure 2A, right two columns).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: Axonal Vax1-immunostaining signals are remarkably decreased in the presence of a rabbit anti-Vax1 polyclonal antibody.
source: These axonal Vax1-immunostaining signals were remarkably decreased in the presence of a rabbit anti-Vax1 polyclonal antibody (α-Vax1) that sequesters Vax1 in the growth medium (Figure 2—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vax1 and Vax1(R152S) proteins are found in the growth medium of transfected COS7 cells.
source: Furthermore, Vax1 and Vax1(R152S) proteins were found in the growth medium of transfected COS7 cells, whereas Vax2 protein was not (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Vax2 protein is not found in the growth medium of transfected COS7 cells.
source: Furthermore, Vax1 and Vax1(R152S) proteins were found in the growth medium of transfected COS7 cells, whereas Vax2 protein was not (Figure 2C).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2C.

claim: Vax1 proteins in the growth medium and co-cultured RGC axons did not originate from dead cells.
source: Since the viability of the transfected COS7 cells were not different from each other (data not shown), these results suggest that Vax1 proteins in the growth medium and co-cultured RGC axons did not originate from dead cells.
evidence: Inferred from cell viability data (not shown) and the differential secretion of Vax1 vs Vax2.

claim: Endogenous Vax1 expressed in vHT explants is detectable in the growth medium.
source: Similar to overexpressed Vax1 in COS7 cells, endogenous Vax1 expressed in vHT explants was detectable in the growth medium (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Vax1 protein is identified in the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) of E14.5 mouse embryos.
source: Furthermore, Vax1 protein was also identified in the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) of E14.5 mouse embryos (Figure 2E), suggesting that Vax1 is secreted in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Vax1 is secreted in vivo as well as in vitro.
source: Furthermore, Vax1 protein was also identified in the cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) of E14.5 mouse embryos (Figure 2E), suggesting that Vax1 is secreted in vivo as well as in vitro.
evidence: Inferred from the detection of Vax1 in CSF and growth medium.

claim: FITC-labeled Vax1-His protein added to the growth medium of retinal explants accumulates in RGC axons.
source: Time-lapse recordings of RGC axons revealed that fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labeled, His-tagged Vax1 (Vax1-His) protein added to the growth medium of retinal explants accumulated in RGC axons and exerted strong growth stimulatory effects on them (Figure 3A,B; Videos 1–3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B, Videos 1–3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: FITC-labeled Vax1-His protein exerts strong growth stimulatory effects on RGC axons.
source: Time-lapse recordings of RGC axons revealed that fluorescein isothiocyanate (FITC)-labeled, His-tagged Vax1 (Vax1-His) protein added to the growth medium of retinal explants accumulated in RGC axons and exerted strong growth stimulatory effects on them (Figure 3A,B; Videos 1–3; Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by time-lapse imaging data shown in Figure 3A,B, Videos 1–3, and Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The axon growth stimulating effects of Vax1-His are applied equally to retinal quadrants.
source: The axon growth stimulating effects of Vax1-His were applied equally to retinal quadrants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), implicating Vax1 is not a region-specific axon growth factor.
evidence: Supported by retinal quadrant explant data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vax1 is not a region-specific axon growth factor.
source: The axon growth stimulating effects of Vax1-His were applied equally to retinal quadrants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2), implicating Vax1 is not a region-specific axon growth factor.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vax1-His stimulates axon growth equally across retinal quadrants.

claim: Vax1(R152S)-His mutant protein is detectable in RGC axons.
source: The transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S)-His mutant protein was also detectable in RGC axons and stimulated axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-His (Figure 3C,D), suggesting that extracellular Vax1 moves to RGC axons and induces axonal growth in transcription-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and axon growth data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Vax1(R152S)-His mutant protein stimulates axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-His.
source: The transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S)-His mutant protein was also detectable in RGC axons and stimulated axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-His (Figure 3C,D), suggesting that extracellular Vax1 moves to RGC axons and induces axonal growth in transcription-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining and axon growth data shown in Figure 3C,D.

claim: Extracellular Vax1 moves to RGC axons and induces axonal growth in transcription-independent manner.
source: The transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S)-His mutant protein was also detectable in RGC axons and stimulated axonal growth as efficiently as WT Vax1-His (Figure 3C,D), suggesting that extracellular Vax1 moves to RGC axons and induces axonal growth in transcription-independent manner.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S) is detectable in axons and stimulates growth.

claim: The ability of recombinant Vax2-His to be internalized and induce RGC axonal growth is almost equivalent to that of Vax1.
source: Despite that Vax2 is not secreted (Figure 2C), the ability of recombinant Vax2-His to be internalized and induce RGC axonal growth is almost equivalent to that of Vax1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), implicating that internalization but not secretion is a conserved characteristic of VAX transcription factors.
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: Internalization but not secretion is a conserved characteristic of VAX transcription factors.
source: Despite that Vax2 is not secreted (Figure 2C), the ability of recombinant Vax2-His to be internalized and induce RGC axonal growth is almost equivalent to that of Vax1 (Figure 3—figure supplement 3), implicating that internalization but not secretion is a conserved characteristic of VAX transcription factors.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both Vax1 and Vax2 can be internalized and induce axon growth when provided exogenously, but only Vax1 is secreted.

claim: Vax1 mRNA is expressed in RGC axon-associated structures, including the OD, the OS, and the vHT, but not the retina, of E14.5 mice.
source: As reported previously (Hallonet et al., 1998; Bertuzzi et al., 1999), Vax1 mRNA is expressed in RGC axon-associated structures, including the OD, the OS, and the vHT, but not the retina, of E14.5 mice (Figure 4A, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data shown in Figure 4A and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A, and cited references (Hallonet et al., 1998; Bertuzzi et al., 1999).

claim: Vax1 protein is detectable in the retina as well as the OS and OD of E14.5 Vax1lacZ/+ heterozygous mouse embryos.
source: However, an examination of Vax1 protein distribution in E14.5 Vax1lacZ/+ heterozygous mouse embryos showed that Vax1 was detectable in the retina as well as the OS and OD (Figure 4B, top row).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: RGCs in Vax1lacZ/+ mice do not express β-gal but do express Vax1.
source: However, we found that RGCs in Vax1lacZ/+ mice did not express β-gal but did express Vax1, this contrasts with OS APCs which co-expressed Vax1 and β-gal (Figure 4B, top row).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: OS APCs in Vax1lacZ/+ mice co-express Vax1 and β-gal.
source: However, we found that RGCs in Vax1lacZ/+ mice did not express β-gal but did express Vax1, this contrasts with OS APCs which co-expressed Vax1 and β-gal (Figure 4B, top row).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Vax1-immunostaining signals are completely absent in RGCs from homozygous lacZ knock-in (Vax1lacZ/lacZ) littermates.
source: Vax1-immunostaining signals were completely absent in RGCs as well as β-gal-positive OS APCs from homozygous lacZ knock-in (Vax1lacZ/lacZ) Vax1lacZ/lacZ littermates, suggesting that Vax1 immunostaining signals in the Vax1lacZ/+ mouse RGC were specific (Figure 4B, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Vax1-immunostaining signals are completely absent in β-gal-positive OS APCs from homozygous lacZ knock-in (Vax1lacZ/lacZ) littermates.
source: Vax1-immunostaining signals were completely absent in RGCs as well as β-gal-positive OS APCs from homozygous lacZ knock-in (Vax1lacZ/lacZ) Vax1lacZ/lacZ littermates, suggesting that Vax1 immunostaining signals in the Vax1lacZ/+ mouse RGC were specific (Figure 4B, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Vax1 immunostaining signals in the Vax1lacZ/+ mouse RGC are specific.
source: Vax1-immunostaining signals were completely absent in RGCs as well as β-gal-positive OS APCs from homozygous lacZ knock-in (Vax1lacZ/lacZ) Vax1lacZ/lacZ littermates, suggesting that Vax1 immunostaining signals in the Vax1lacZ/+ mouse RGC were specific (Figure 4B, bottom row).
evidence: Inferred from the absence of Vax1 immunostaining in Vax1lacZ/lacZ mice.

claim: Vax1 protein in RGCs might originate from the neighboring Vax1/β-gal double-positive APCs in the OS or NPCs and radial glia in the vHT.
source: Collectively, these data demonstrate that Vax1 protein in RGCs might originate from the neighboring Vax1/β-gal double-positive APCs in the OS or NPCs and radial glia in the vHT (Figure 4B, Figure 4—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that RGCs express Vax1 protein but not Vax1 mRNA or β-gal, while neighboring cells express both Vax1 and β-gal.

claim: Vax1 protein in OS APCs is present mainly in nuclei.
source: Vax1 protein in OS APCs was present mainly in nuclei, whereas a majority of Vax1 protein in β-gal-negative RGCs was non-nuclear (Figure 4B, i and ii).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: A majority of Vax1 protein in β-gal-negative RGCs is non-nuclear.
source: Vax1 protein in OS APCs was present mainly in nuclei, whereas a majority of Vax1 protein in β-gal-negative RGCs was non-nuclear (Figure 4B, i and ii).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B.

claim: Vax1 co-localizes with NF160 in E14.5 WT mouse RGC axons.
source: Furthermore, Vax1 co-localized with NF160 in E14.5 WT mouse RGC axons but was lost in Vax1lacZ/lacZ mouse RGC axons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Vax1 is lost in Vax1lacZ/lacZ mouse RGC axons.
source: Furthermore, Vax1 co-localized with NF160 in E14.5 WT mouse RGC axons but was lost in Vax1lacZ/lacZ mouse RGC axons (Figure 4C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4C.

claim: Vax1 protein is highly enriched at the extracellular part of the RGC membrane.
source: Vax1 protein was highly enriched at the extracellular part of the RGC membrane and was also detected in the cytoplasm and intracellular vesicles (Figure 4D, top row; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immuno-transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vax1 protein is detected in the cytoplasm and intracellular vesicles of RGCs.
source: Vax1 protein was highly enriched at the extracellular part of the RGC membrane and was also detected in the cytoplasm and intracellular vesicles (Figure 4D, top row; Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immuno-transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D and Figure 4—figure supplement 2.

claim: Vax1 protein in OS APCs is enriched in nuclei.
source: Vax1 protein in OS APCs was not only enriched in nuclei but was also detectable in cytoplasmic membrane structures (Figure 4D, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by immuno-transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: Vax1 protein in OS APCs is detectable in cytoplasmic membrane structures.
source: Vax1 protein in OS APCs was not only enriched in nuclei but was also detectable in cytoplasmic membrane structures (Figure 4D, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by immuno-transmission electron microscopy data shown in Figure 4D.

claim: OS- and/or vHT-secreted Vax1 might enter RGCs after docking with the RGC axon membrane.
source: These results therefore suggest that OS- and/or vHT-secreted Vax1 might enter RGCs after docking with the RGC axon membrane.
evidence: Inferred from the localization patterns of Vax1 in RGCs and OS APCs observed by electron microscopy.

claim: α-Vax1 interferes with the transfer of Vax1 from vHT cells to RGC axons.
source: α-Vax1 not only interfered with the transfer of Vax1 from vHT cells to RGC axons, it also antagonized RGC axonal growth toward vHT explants (Figure 5A, center).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: α-Vax1 antagonizes RGC axonal growth toward vHT explants.
source: α-Vax1 not only interfered with the transfer of Vax1 from vHT cells to RGC axons, it also antagonized RGC axonal growth toward vHT explants (Figure 5A, center).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neither rb-IgG nor α-Vax2 influences Vax1 transfer into RGC axons.
source: In contrast, neither rb-IgG (pre-immune rabbit IgG) nor α-Vax2 influenced Vax1 transfer into RGC axons or RGC axonal growth toward vHT explants (Figure 5A, left and right).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Neither rb-IgG nor α-Vax2 influences RGC axonal growth toward vHT explants.
source: In contrast, neither rb-IgG (pre-immune rabbit IgG) nor α-Vax2 influenced Vax1 transfer into RGC axons or RGC axonal growth toward vHT explants (Figure 5A, left and right).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 5A.

claim: α-Vax1 treatment reduces the population of retinal axons growing toward the vHT.
source: α-Vax1 treatment not only reduced the population of retinal axons growing toward the vHT (Figure 5B), it also decreased the total number of retinal axons growing from the explants (Figure 5C), suggesting an axogenic activity as well as an axon growth-stimulating activity of extracellular Vax1.
evidence: Supported by axon count data shown in Figure 5B.

claim: α-Vax1 treatment decreases the total number of retinal axons growing from the explants.
source: α-Vax1 treatment not only reduced the population of retinal axons growing toward the vHT (Figure 5B), it also decreased the total number of retinal axons growing from the explants (Figure 5C), suggesting an axogenic activity as well as an axon growth-stimulating activity of extracellular Vax1.
evidence: Supported by axon count data shown in Figure 5C.

claim: Extracellular Vax1 has axogenic activity.
source: α-Vax1 treatment not only reduced the population of retinal axons growing toward the vHT (Figure 5B), it also decreased the total number of retinal axons growing from the explants (Figure 5C), suggesting an axogenic activity as well as an axon growth-stimulating activity of extracellular Vax1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that α-Vax1 decreases the total number of axons.

claim: Extracellular Vax1 has axon growth-stimulating activity.
source: α-Vax1 treatment not only reduced the population of retinal axons growing toward the vHT (Figure 5B), it also decreased the total number of retinal axons growing from the explants (Figure 5C), suggesting an axogenic activity as well as an axon growth-stimulating activity of extracellular Vax1.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that α-Vax1 reduces axon growth toward vHT.

claim: Mouse embryos implanted with α-Vax1-releasing gels show a remarkable reduction in RGC axons accessing the midline compared with embryos implanted with rb-IgG-releasing gels.
source: Mouse embryos implanted with α-Vax1-releasing gels showed a remarkable reduction in RGC axons accessing the midline compared with embryos implanted with rb-IgG-releasing gels (Figure 5D).
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 5D.

claim: In α-Vax1-implanted mouse embryos, a significant number of RGC axons show reduced Vax1 immunoreactivity and stop at the lateral wall of the ventral diencephalon.
source: In α-Vax1-implanted mouse embryos, a significant number of RGC axons showed reduced Vax1 immunoreactivity and stopped at the lateral wall of the ventral diencephalon, properties similar to those observed in Vax1−/− mice (Bertuzzi et al., 1999) (Figure 5D, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 5D and cited reference (Bertuzzi et al., 1999).

claim: Extracellular Vax1 is necessary for RGC axonal growth to the ventral midline.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that extracellular Vax1 is necessary for RGC axonal growth to the ventral midline.
evidence: Inferred from the in vitro and in vivo experiments showing that sequestering extracellular Vax1 reduces RGC axon growth toward the midline.

claim: HSPGs, including Sdc2, Sdc3, and glypican 1 (Glp1), are highly expressed in mouse RGC axons.
source: HSPGs, including Sdc2, Sdc3, and glypican 1 (Glp1), are highly expressed in mouse RGC axons and have been proposed to play critical roles in RGC axon guidance in various vertebrates (Chung et al., 2001; Inatani et al., 2003; Lee and Chien, 2004; Pratt et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Chung et al., 2001; Inatani et al., 2003; Lee and Chien, 2004; Pratt et al., 2006).

claim: HSPGs have been proposed to play critical roles in RGC axon guidance in various vertebrates.
source: HSPGs, including Sdc2, Sdc3, and glypican 1 (Glp1), are highly expressed in mouse RGC axons and have been proposed to play critical roles in RGC axon guidance in various vertebrates (Chung et al., 2001; Inatani et al., 2003; Lee and Chien, 2004; Pratt et al., 2006).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Chung et al., 2001; Inatani et al., 2003; Lee and Chien, 2004; Pratt et al., 2006).

claim: The transfer of Vax1-EGFP to neighboring wing disc cells is suppressed upon co-expression of Sdc in the A/P boundary cells.
source: However, the transfer of Vax1-EGFP to neighboring wing disc cells was suppressed upon co-expression of Sdc in the A/P boundary cells (Figure 6, third row).
evidence: Supported by Drosophila wing disc imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Overexpressed Dlp suppresses Vax1 transfer in the same manner as Sdc.
source: Overexpressed dally-like protein (Dlp), a Drosophila homolog of Glp, also suppressed Vax1 transfer in the same manner as Sdc (Figure 6, bottom row), suggesting that the intercellular transfer of Vax1 in Drosophila wing imaginal disc cells is mediated by HSPGs but not specifically by Sdc.
evidence: Supported by Drosophila wing disc imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: The intercellular transfer of Vax1 in Drosophila wing imaginal disc cells is mediated by HSPGs but not specifically by Sdc.
source: Overexpressed dally-like protein (Dlp), a Drosophila homolog of Glp, also suppressed Vax1 transfer in the same manner as Sdc (Figure 6, bottom row), suggesting that the intercellular transfer of Vax1 in Drosophila wing imaginal disc cells is mediated by HSPGs but not specifically by Sdc.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that both Sdc and Dlp suppress Vax1 transfer.

claim: Overexpressed HSPGs in the A/P boundary cells capture co-expressed Vax1-EGFP protein, thereby interfering with the transfer of Vax1-EGFP to neighboring cells.
source: These results also imply that these overexpressed HSPGs in the A/P boundary cells captured co-expressed Vax1-EGFP protein, thereby interfering with the transfer of Vax1-EGFP to neighboring cells (Figure 6, diagram in the right column).
evidence: Inferred from the observation that overexpression of HSPGs reduces Vax1 transfer to neighboring cells.

claim: Vax1-EGFP proteins are transferred farther in the Sdc mutant (Sdc23) wing imaginal disc.
source: Conversely, Vax1-EGFP proteins were transferred farther in the Sdc mutant (Sdc23) wing imaginal disc, where total HSPG levels were reduced owing to the loss of Sdc (Figure 6, second row).
evidence: Supported by Drosophila wing disc imaging data shown in Figure 6.

claim: Vax1 interacts with Sdc2 in E14.5 mouse optic nerves.
source: We found that Vax1, but not Vax2, interacted with Sdc2 in E14.5 mouse optic nerves as well as with overexpressed Sdc1 and Sdc2 in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Vax1 interacts with overexpressed Sdc1 in HEK 293T cells.
source: We found that Vax1, but not Vax2, interacted with Sdc2 in E14.5 mouse optic nerves as well as with overexpressed Sdc1 and Sdc2 in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Vax1 interacts with overexpressed Sdc2 in HEK 293T cells.
source: We found that Vax1, but not Vax2, interacted with Sdc2 in E14.5 mouse optic nerves as well as with overexpressed Sdc1 and Sdc2 in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Vax2 does not interact with Sdc2 in E14.5 mouse optic nerves.
source: We found that Vax1, but not Vax2, interacted with Sdc2 in E14.5 mouse optic nerves as well as with overexpressed Sdc1 and Sdc2 in human embryonic kidney (HEK) 293T cells (Figure 7A, Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7A and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Sdc2-N, lacking the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain, is able to interact with Vax1.
source: Sdc2-N, lacking the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain, was able to interact with Vax1, whereas Sdc2-C, which lacks the N-terminal extracellular domain, failed to interact with Vax1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Vax1 binds to the extracellular domain of Sdc.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Sdc2-C, which lacks the N-terminal extracellular domain, fails to interact with Vax1.
source: Sdc2-N, lacking the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain, was able to interact with Vax1, whereas Sdc2-C, which lacks the N-terminal extracellular domain, failed to interact with Vax1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Vax1 binds to the extracellular domain of Sdc.
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Vax1 binds to the extracellular domain of Sdc.
source: Sdc2-N, lacking the C-terminal cytoplasmic domain, was able to interact with Vax1, whereas Sdc2-C, which lacks the N-terminal extracellular domain, failed to interact with Vax1 (Figure 7—figure supplement 1C), suggesting that Vax1 binds to the extracellular domain of Sdc.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Sdc2-N (with extracellular domain) interacts with Vax1 while Sdc2-C (without extracellular domain) does not.

claim: Vax1 interactions with Sdc2, Sdc3, and Glp1 expressed in RGC axons in E14.5 optic nerves are disrupted in the presence of free heparin.
source: Vax1 interactions with each of these HSPGs expressed in RGC axons in E14.5 optic nerves were disrupted in the presence of free heparin, whereas interactions with Pax2 (paired homeobox 2), which complexes with Vax1 in OS APCs, were not (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Vax1 interactions with Pax2 are not disrupted in the presence of free heparin.
source: Vax1 interactions with each of these HSPGs expressed in RGC axons in E14.5 optic nerves were disrupted in the presence of free heparin, whereas interactions with Pax2 (paired homeobox 2), which complexes with Vax1 in OS APCs, were not (Figure 7B).
evidence: Supported by co-immunoprecipitation data shown in Figure 7B.

claim: Recombinant Vax1-His specifically binds HS-sepharose resin with high affinity.
source: Moreover, recombinant Vax1-His specifically bound HS-sepharose resin with high affinity (Figure 7C).
evidence: Supported by resin binding assay data shown in Figure 7C.

claim: Vax1 preferentially binds to HS side chains of HSPG proteins expressed in RGC axons.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that Vax1 preferentially binds to HS side chains of HSPG proteins expressed in RGC axons.
evidence: Inferred from the heparin competition assay and HS-sepharose binding assay.

claim: Sdc3 is expressed in E14.5 mouse RGCs in a non-polarized manner.
source: Sdc3 was expressed in E14.5 mouse RGCs in a non-polarized manner and co-localized with Vax1 in RGC axons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: Sdc3 co-localizes with Vax1 in RGC axons.
source: Sdc3 was expressed in E14.5 mouse RGCs in a non-polarized manner and co-localized with Vax1 in RGC axons (Figure 7—figure supplement 2).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 2.

claim: The growth stimulatory effects of Vax1 on RGC axons are abolished by the treatment of retinal explants with heparinase I.
source: The growth stimulatory effects of Vax1 on RGC axons were abolished by the treatment of retinal explants with heparinase I, which cleaves heparin and HS sugar chains, but not by incubation with chondroitinase ABC (ChnaseABC), which digests chondroitin sugar chains (Bishop et al., 2007; Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by retinal explant treatment data shown in Figure 7D,E and cited reference (Bishop et al., 2007).

claim: The growth stimulatory effects of Vax1 on RGC axons are not abolished by incubation with chondroitinase ABC (ChnaseABC).
source: The growth stimulatory effects of Vax1 on RGC axons were abolished by the treatment of retinal explants with heparinase I, which cleaves heparin and HS sugar chains, but not by incubation with chondroitinase ABC (ChnaseABC), which digests chondroitin sugar chains (Bishop et al., 2007; Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by retinal explant treatment data shown in Figure 7D,E and cited reference (Bishop et al., 2007).

claim: Heparinase I treatment decreases the immunostaining intensity of exogenously provided Vax1-His in RGC axons.
source: Heparinase I treatment also decreased the immunostaining intensity of exogenously provided Vax1-His in RGC axons (Figure 7D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: Neither heparinase I nor ChnaseABC influences RGC axon growth in the absence of Vax1.
source: Neither heparinase I nor ChnaseABC influenced RGC axon growth in the absence of Vax1 (Figure 7D,E).
evidence: Supported by retinal explant treatment data shown in Figure 7D,E.

claim: The binding of Vax1 to HSPGs is necessary for the induction of RGC axonal growth.
source: Collectively, these results suggest that the binding of Vax1 to HSPGs is necessary for the induction of RGC axonal growth.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that heparinase I treatment abolishes Vax1-induced RGC axon growth.

claim: Vax1(WF/SR) mutant lacks the ability to cross the cell membrane but remains capable of binding to Sdc2.
source: To answer this question, we tested the function of a Vax1(WF/SR) mutant, in which conserved Trp147 and Phe148 amino acids responsible for cell penetration were replaced with Ser167 and Arg148 (Joliot et al., 1998); this mutant lacks the ability to cross the cell membrane but remains capable of binding to Sdc2 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: Supported by cell penetration and binding assay data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1A,B and cited reference (Joliot et al., 1998).

claim: Vax1(WF/SR) barely penetrates RGC axons.
source: We found that Vax1(WF/SR) barely penetrated RGC axons and induced RGC axonal growth less efficiently than WT Vax1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Vax1(WF/SR) induces RGC axonal growth less efficiently than WT Vax1.
source: We found that Vax1(WF/SR) barely penetrated RGC axons and induced RGC axonal growth less efficiently than WT Vax1 (Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1C,D.

claim: Vax1-induced RGC axonal growth requires cell penetration.
source: These results suggest that Vax1-induced RGC axonal growth requires cell penetration.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that cell penetration-defective Vax1(WF/SR) induces RGC axonal growth less efficiently than WT Vax1.

claim: A majority of proteins isolated by Vax1-affinity purification are related to protein synthesis.
source: Interestingly, a majority of proteins isolated by Vax1-affinity purification were related to protein synthesis, including ribosomal proteins (RPs) L11, L23A, L26, S14, and S16; translation regulators, such as eukaryotic translation initiation factor (eIF) 3B and 3C; and the chaperone HSPA1A (heat shock 70-kDa protein 1A).
evidence: Supported by MALDI-TOF mass spectrometry analysis of Vax1-affinity purified proteins shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Vax1 might act in RGC axons by modulating protein synthesis.
source: These data suggest that Vax1 might act in RGC axons by modulating protein synthesis, a mechanism similar to that by which cytoplasmic En2 controls RGC axonal growth (Brunet et al., 2005; Yoon et al., 2012).
evidence: Inferred from the identification of protein synthesis-related proteins in Vax1 complexes, and supported by cited references (Brunet et al., 2005; Yoon et al., 2012).

claim: Treatment with Vax1-His induces a remarkable increase in the fluorescence intensities of AHA-Fluor 488-labeled proteins in RGC axons.
source: Treatment with Vax1-His induced a remarkable increase in the fluorescence intensities of AHA-Fluor 488-labeled proteins in RGC axons (Figure 8B, middle column), whereas the Vax1(WF/SR)-His had no effect on protein synthesis (Figure 8B, right column), indicating that intracellular Vax1 stimulated protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by AHA labeling data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Vax1(WF/SR)-His has no effect on protein synthesis in RGC axons.
source: Treatment with Vax1-His induced a remarkable increase in the fluorescence intensities of AHA-Fluor 488-labeled proteins in RGC axons (Figure 8B, middle column), whereas the Vax1(WF/SR)-His had no effect on protein synthesis (Figure 8B, right column), indicating that intracellular Vax1 stimulated protein synthesis.
evidence: Supported by AHA labeling data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Intracellular Vax1 stimulates protein synthesis.
source: Treatment with Vax1-His induced a remarkable increase in the fluorescence intensities of AHA-Fluor 488-labeled proteins in RGC axons (Figure 8B, middle column), whereas the Vax1(WF/SR)-His had no effect on protein synthesis (Figure 8B, right column), indicating that intracellular Vax1 stimulated protein synthesis.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vax1-His increases AHA-labeled protein fluorescence while cell penetration-defective Vax1(WF/SR)-His does not.

claim: Vax1-His-induced effects on AHA-Fluor 488 fluorescence intensities in retinal cell bodies are not notably different from those of Vax1(WF/SR)-His or the 6X-His.
source: In contrast to its significant induction of protein synthesis in axons, Vax1-His-induced effects on AHA-Fluor 488 fluorescence intensities in retinal cell bodies were not notably different from those of Vax1(WF/SR)-His or the 6X-His (Figure 8B, bottom row).
evidence: Supported by AHA labeling data shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Isolated retinal axons from the cell body still respond to Vax1 as efficiently as those that project from intact retinal explants.
source: In contrast, isolated retinal axons from the cell body still responded to Vax1 as efficiently as those that projected from intact retinal explants (Figure 8C,D).
evidence: Supported by isolated axon treatment data shown in Figure 8C,D.

claim: Vax1 stimulates RGC axon growth by stimulating local translation of specific mRNA in the axon rather than by modulating gene expression in the cell body.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Vax1 stimulates RGC axon growth by stimulating local translation of specific mRNA in the axon rather than by modulating gene expression in the cell body.
evidence: Inferred from the observations that Vax1 increases protein synthesis in axons but not cell bodies, and that isolated axons respond to Vax1.

claim: Remarkable numbers of RGC axons are detectable in the vHT of Vax1−/− mouse embryos implanted with collagen gels that release recombinant Vax1-His.
source: In contrast to the lack of RGC axon access to the vHT observed in Vax1−/− mouse embryos, remarkable numbers of RGC axons were detectable in the vHT of Vax1−/− mouse embryos implanted with collagen gels that released recombinant Vax1-His (Figure 9A, top rows of left two columns, B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Remarkable number of RGC axons are able to grow to the source of extracellular Vax1 protein (i.e., the third ventricle), although they fail to restore the OC.
source: Remarkable number of RGC axons were able to grow to the source of extracellular Vax1 protein (i.e., the third ventricle), although they failed to restore the OC.
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Implantation of collagen gels that release cell-penetration–defective Vax1(WF/SR)-His does not induce the regrowth of RGC axons.
source: In contrast, implantation of collagen gels that released cell-penetration–defective Vax1(WF/SR)-His did not induce the regrowth of RGC axons (Figure 9A, [third column], B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Implanted recombinant Vax1-His is detectable in RGC axons.
source: Implanted recombinant Vax1-His was detectable in RGC axons, whereas Vax1(WF/SR)-His was not, suggesting that the implanted Vax1 stimulated RGC axon growth by penetrating into the axoplasm.
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: Implanted Vax1(WF/SR)-His is not detectable in RGC axons.
source: Implanted recombinant Vax1-His was detectable in RGC axons, whereas Vax1(WF/SR)-His was not, suggesting that the implanted Vax1 stimulated RGC axon growth by penetrating into the axoplasm.
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A.

claim: The implanted Vax1 stimulates RGC axon growth by penetrating into the axoplasm.
source: Implanted recombinant Vax1-His was detectable in RGC axons, whereas Vax1(WF/SR)-His was not, suggesting that the implanted Vax1 stimulated RGC axon growth by penetrating into the axoplasm.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Vax1-His, but not cell penetration-defective Vax1(WF/SR)-His, is detectable in axons and induces axon growth.

claim: The growth of RGC axons towards Vax1−/− vHT explants is partly recovered by sequestering extracellular Slit protein using Robo1-Fc.
source: In support of this, the growth of RGC axons towards Vax1−/− vHT explants were partly recovered by sequestering extracellular Slit protein using an Fc-fused extracellular fragment of the Slit receptor Robo1 (Robo1-Fc) (Figure 9—figure supplement 1).
evidence: Supported by co-culture explant data shown in Figure 9—figure supplement 1.

claim: The growth of RGC axons into the vHT is partially rescued by implanting a Robo1-Fc–releasing collagen gel into the third ventricle.
source: The growth of RGC axons into the vHT was partially rescued by implanting a Robo1-Fc–releasing collagen gel into the third ventricle, an effect that was further enhanced by implantation of gels co-releasing Vax1-His and Robo1-Fc (Figure 9A, two right columns, B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: The rescue of RGC axon growth into the vHT by Robo1-Fc is further enhanced by implantation of gels co-releasing Vax1-His and Robo1-Fc.
source: The growth of RGC axons into the vHT was partially rescued by implanting a Robo1-Fc–releasing collagen gel into the third ventricle, an effect that was further enhanced by implantation of gels co-releasing Vax1-His and Robo1-Fc (Figure 9A, two right columns, B).
evidence: Supported by in vivo collagen gel implantation data shown in Figure 9A,B.

claim: Vax1 possesses a novel RGC axon growth factor activity that is critical for the development of the mammalian binocular visual system.
source: Together, our findings demonstrate that Vax1 possesses a novel RGC axon growth factor activity that is critical for the development of the mammalian binocular visual system.
evidence: Inferred from all the experimental findings showing that Vax1 is secreted, binds to HSPGs, penetrates axons, stimulates local protein synthesis, and promotes RGC axon growth.

claim: Vax1 plays an essential role in the development of the OC by regulating RGC axon growth in a non-cell autonomous manner.
source: Ventral anterior homeobox 1 (Vax1) plays an essential role in the development of the OC by regulating RGC axon growth in a non-cell autonomous manner.
evidence: Supported by the co-culture explant experiments and in vivo rescue experiments.

claim: Vax1 is secreted from ventral hypothalamic cells and diffuses to RGC axons.
source: In this study, we identify an unexpected function of Vax1 that is secreted from ventral hypothalamic cells and diffuses to RGC axons, where it promotes axonal growth independent of its transcription factor activity.
evidence: Supported by Western blot detection of Vax1 in growth medium and CSF, and immunostaining showing Vax1 in RGC axons.

claim: Vax1 promotes axonal growth independent of its transcription factor activity.
source: In this study, we identify an unexpected function of Vax1 that is secreted from ventral hypothalamic cells and diffuses to RGC axons, where it promotes axonal growth independent of its transcription factor activity.
evidence: Supported by the observation that transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S) promotes RGC axon growth as efficiently as WT Vax1.

claim: Vax1 binds to extracellular sugar groups of the heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) located in RGC axons.
source: We demonstrate that Vax1 binds to extracellular sugar groups of the heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs) located in RGC axons.
evidence: Supported by heparin competition assays, HS-sepharose binding assays, and co-immunoprecipitation experiments.

claim: Both Vax1 binding to HSPGs and subsequent penetration into the axoplasm are required for RGC axonal growth.
source: Both Vax1 binding to HSPGs and subsequent penetration into the axoplasm, where Vax1 activates local protein synthesis, are required for RGC axonal growth.
evidence: Supported by experiments showing that heparinase I treatment or cell penetration-defective Vax1(WF/SR) mutant abolishes RGC axon growth.

claim: Vax1 activates local protein synthesis in the axoplasm.
source: Both Vax1 binding to HSPGs and subsequent penetration into the axoplasm, where Vax1 activates local protein synthesis, are required for RGC axonal growth.
evidence: Supported by AHA labeling experiments showing increased protein synthesis in axons treated with Vax1-His.

claim: Vax1 is a homeodomain transcription factor expressed in various ventral-medial forebrain-derived structures.
source: Ventral anterior homeobox 1 (Vax1) is a homeodomain transcription factor expressed in various ventral-medial forebrain-derived structures, including the medial and lateral geniculate eminences, the ventral septum, the anterior entopeduncular area, the preoptic area, the vHT, and the OS (Hallonet et al., 1998; Bertuzzi et al., 1999).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Hallonet et al., 1998; Bertuzzi et al., 1999).

claim: Genetic inactivation of Vax1 in humans and mice causes agenesis of multiple midline structures of the brain.
source: Genetic inactivation of Vax1 in humans and mice causes agenesis of multiple midline structures of the brain, including the anterior commissure, the corpus callosum, and the OC, in addition to the coloboma of the eye (Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Hallonet et al., 1999; Slavotinek et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by cited references (Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Hallonet et al., 1999; Slavotinek et al., 2012).

claim: RGC axons in Vax1-deficient mice can grow through the OS but cannot access the vHT area and fail to form an OC.
source: RGC axons in Vax1-deficient mice can grow through the OS but cannot access the vHT area and fail to form an OC.
evidence: Supported by cited references (Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Mui et al., 2005) and experimental observations.

claim: Vax1 is not expressed in RGCs despite its critical roles in growth and fasciculation of RGC axons.
source: Vax1 is not expressed in RGCs despite its critical roles in growth and fasciculation of RGC axons (Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Mui et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by in situ hybridization data and cited references (Bertuzzi et al., 1999; Mui et al., 2005).

claim: Defects in OC formation in Vax1-deficient mouse RGCs might be caused by the loss or gain of axon guidance cues that are potential transcription targets of Vax1 in vHT cells.
source: Therefore, it has been suggested that defects in OC formation in Vax1-deficient mouse RGCs might be caused by the loss or gain of axon guidance cues that are potential transcription targets of Vax1 in vHT cells.
evidence: This was a prior hypothesis that the current study challenges.

claim: Vax1 promotes RGC axon growth in a transcription-independent manner.
source: Contrary to expectation, we here found that Vax1 promoted RGC axon growth in a transcription-independent manner.
evidence: Supported by experiments with transcriptionally inactive Vax1(R152S) mutant.

claim: Vax1 is secreted from vHT cells and binds and enters RGC axons to stimulate axonal growth.
source: Moreover, Vax1 is secreted from vHT cells and binds and enters RGC axons to stimulate axonal growth.
evidence: Supported by Western blot, immunostaining, and functional assays.

claim: The trafficking of Vax1 to RGC axons is mediated by heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs), such as syndecan and glypican, expressed in RGC axons.
source: This unexpected trafficking of Vax1 to RGC axons was mediated by heparan sulfate proteoglycans (HSPGs), such as syndecan and glypican, expressed in RGC axons.
evidence: Supported by Drosophila experiments, co-immunoprecipitation, and heparinase treatment experiments.

claim: Vax1 binding to HSPGs is not sufficient to trigger RGC axon growth; penetration into the RGC axoplasm and subsequent stimulation of local protein synthesis are also necessary.
source: However, Vax1 binding to HSPGs was not sufficient to trigger RGC axon growth; penetration into the RGC axoplasm and subsequent stimulation of local protein synthesis were also necessary.
evidence: Supported by experiments with cell penetration-defective Vax1(WF/SR) mutant and AHA labeling experiments.

claim: Vax1 possesses a novel RGC axon growth factor activity that enables RGC axons to grow toward the midline during development.
source: Taken together, our findings reveal an unconventional function of Vax1 as an RGC axon growth factor that enables RGC axons to grow toward the midline during development.
evidence: Inferred from all the experimental findings.
